cards.explanation: The answer is that Paul begs that he won't need to be as bold as he expects. He writes to the Corinthians, "I beg you that when I come I may not need to be as bold as I expect toward those who presume that we live according to the flesh." (2 Corinthians 10:2) He's hoping for a gentle visit, friends. I think he'd much rather show up and share cookies than give a lecture.

The answer is False. Paul says, "The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the flesh." (2 Corinthians 10:4) Then he tells us what they are instead: weapons with divine power. He's not swinging a rolling pin here, friends.

The answer is divine. Paul says the weapons of our warfare "…have divine power to demolish strongholds." (2 Corinthians 10:4) The power isn't from us, friends. It comes from God, and that's why the weapons work.

The answer is to make it obedient to Christ. Paul says, "…we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:5) The point isn't winning, friends. It's obedience to Christ. Even my wandering thoughts about the cookie jar need to hear that.

The answer is the Corinthians' obedience. Paul says they'll be ready to punish disobedience "…as soon as your obedience is complete." (2 Corinthians 10:6) So the timing hangs on the Corinthians' obedience being complete. That's a lot of patience, friends, if you ask me.

The answer is True. Paul says anyone confident that he belongs to Christ "…should remind himself that we belong to Christ just as much as he does." (2 Corinthians 10:7) Nobody gets to claim Christ all to themselves, friends. Paul belongs to Him too.

The answer is False. Paul says the Lord gave him authority "…for building you up rather than tearing you down…" (2 Corinthians 10:8) It's for building up, friends, not tearing down. Think of a good baker's helper who adds to the batch instead of knocking over the cooling rack.

The answer is unimpressive. Some say, "His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account." (2 Corinthians 10:10) Ouch, friends. That's quite a review. I know a little about being called unimpressive, back when I was a stamper in a junk drawer.

The answer is that in person the actions will match the letters. Paul says, "…what we are in our letters when absent, we will be in our actions when present." (2 Corinthians 10:11) His words on paper and his actions in person will line up, friends. What you read is what you get.

The answer is ignorance. Paul says, "When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance." (2 Corinthians 10:12) Those folks are measuring themselves by themselves, friends. Paul calls that ignorance.

The answer is True. Paul says he'll boast only "…within the field of influence that God has assigned to us…" and he says that field reaches even to the Corinthians. (2 Corinthians 10:13) The Corinthians are inside that field, friends. Paul isn't reaching into someone else's yard.

The answer is that the gospel first reached them through Paul. He says, "…we were the first to reach you with the gospel of Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:14) Since he got there first, friends, he isn't overstepping. That's his reason, straight from the text.

The answer is Paul's influence among them. Paul writes, "…we hope that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you will greatly increase as well…" (2 Corinthians 10:15) That's his hope, friends, and it's tied to their faith growing. What he hopes will increase is his influence among them.

The answer is so he can preach in the regions beyond them. Paul hopes his influence grows "…so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you." (2 Corinthians 10:16) He wants to keep going and reach new places, friends. Corinth isn't the finish line.
The answer is Lord. Paul says, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." (2 Corinthians 10:17) He's quoting Jeremiah (Jeremiah 9:24). If there's a boast to be made, friends, it goes to the Lord.

The answer is False. Paul says, "…it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends." (2 Corinthians 10:18) Self-praise doesn't count, friends. The Lord's approval does.
